name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: A silver cup at 100
items.fact: Since 1963, the Japanese government has sent a silver sake cup to everyone who turns 100. As the number of centenarians grew, it switched to a cheaper silver-plated cup to save money.

items.name: A card from the King
items.fact: In the UK, people who reach their 100th birthday can receive a card from the King, then another at 105 and every year after that. Couples can get one for their 60th wedding anniversary.

items.name: The Centenarian Bounty
items.fact: In Ireland, everyone who turns 100 receives a letter from the President and a cheque known as the “Centenarian Bounty”. People who reach 101 and beyond get a special coin every year.

items.name: Kajimaya
items.fact: In Okinawa, the 97th birthday is celebrated with “kajimaya”: the birthday person is driven through the neighbourhood, often in an open car, holding a pinwheel, a symbol of becoming a child again.

items.name: Kanreki
items.fact: In Japan, turning 60 is called “kanreki”, the return to the start of the calendar cycle. The birthday person traditionally wears a red waistcoat and hat, like a baby starting life again.

items.name: Selling your home “en viager”
items.fact: In France you can sell your home “en viager”: the buyer pays a lump sum and then a monthly amount until you die, while you keep living there. One famous buyer paid for thirty years and died first.

items.name: Students in a care home
items.fact: A care home in Deventer, in the Netherlands, lets university students live there rent-free. In return, they spend time with the older residents: watching football, celebrating birthdays or just chatting.

items.name: A toast to 100
items.fact: In Sardinia, an island with a remarkable number of people over 100, a traditional toast is “A kent’annos”, which means “May you live to be 100”.

items.name: The autumn-leaf sticker
items.fact: In Japan, older drivers put a special sticker on their car so that other drivers give them more space. The original design, shaped like a falling autumn leaf, gave it its nickname.

items.name: A walking stick at 100
items.fact: In South Korea, people who turn 100 receive a traditional walking stick, the “cheongnyeojang”, from the government, on the country’s Day for Older Persons in October.

fakes.name: The golden bell
fakes.fact: Dutch towns give a golden bicycle bell to anyone who still cycles to the town hall on their 90th birthday. The mayor fits it to the bike personally, and the local paper takes a photo.

fakes.name: A free birthday cake
fakes.fact: An Italian law from 1972 says that a bakery must give a free cake to any customer who can prove that they turn 100 that day. Most bakers say they have never been asked.

fakes.name: Your face on a stamp
fakes.fact: Sweden’s postal service prints a personal stamp with the face of every person who turns 100. Families get a sheet of fifty, and many use them for the party invitations.

fakes.name: The church key
fakes.fact: In many Flemish villages, the oldest resident keeps the church key and opens the doors on Christmas Eve. If they are too frail, they choose a grandchild to do it for them.

fakes.name: A birch tree at 100
fakes.fact: Finland plants a birch tree for every citizen who reaches 100 in a “centenarians’ forest” near Helsinki. Each tree has a small metal plate with the person’s name and birthday.

fakes.name: A hundred bells
fakes.fact: In some Swiss villages, the church bells ring a hundred times at noon when a resident turns 100. Neighbours count the rings, and the birthday person drinks the first glass of wine.

fakes.name: The first vote
fakes.fact: In Portuguese villages, the oldest voter traditionally casts the first vote on election day, and the polling station waits to open until they arrive or send word that they aren’t coming.

fakes.name: Name a street
fakes.fact: Iceland lets every person who turns 100 choose the name of a new street in their town. One street in a fishing town is named after a centenarian’s favourite dog.

fakes.name: A second coming-of-age day
fakes.fact: Japanese towns hold a “second coming-of-age day” for residents turning 80. They wear the same style of kimono as the twenty-year-olds and give a short speech about their life.

fakes.name: Free trains at 100
fakes.fact: Germany lets anyone over 100 travel free in first class on every train in the country, with one companion. Fewer than 200 people a year actually use the pass.

fake: Give it a real-sounding name, maybe a word in the local language.
Something surprising but possible: a gift, a ceremony, a law or a habit.
A real country, region or town.
The birthday or the stage of life when it happens.
The family, the neighbours, the town, the government.
A number, a date, a cost or a small problem with it.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“most people forget to ask for it”): perfect things sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
